A research paper, explained for everyone

Teaching a computer to remove window reflections by practising on over a million realistic fake ones

An Adobe system that cleans reflections out of RAW photos, trained only on simulated reflections, with an optional 'look behind you' photo as a hint

Based on the paper: Removing Reflections from RAW Photos · Eric Kee, Adam Pikielny, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Marc Levoy (Adobe Inc.) · arXiv:2404.14414 (v3) 2025

🧒 In kid words

When you take a picture through a window, you also catch a ghost picture of what is behind you. This computer learned to peel that ghost off by practicing on lots of pretend ghosts that were made just like real ones.

📖 The short version

When you photograph through a window, the glass adds a faint picture of what is behind you on top of your subject. The authors made over a million realistic fake reflections by adding real photos together while their pixel numbers still measured light, before the camera's color and brightness finishing, and trained a program on those alone. It removes reflections from real RAW photos at full resolution and hands back the reflection as a separate layer you can edit.

🔬 For experts

Mixtures m = t + r are synthesized from RAW sources in linear XYZ before white balance, with Fresnel attenuation, pose, double reflection and defocus, then filtered for visibility; models train from scratch on 1,241,091 mixtures with no real-image fine-tuning. A 2.5M-parameter base model at 256p, optionally modulated by an unaligned context photo, feeds a mask-based Gaussian-pyramid upsampler. On the authors' simulated RAW test set, retraining Zhang, DSRNet and Zhu on this data raised their SSIMt improvement over control by about 40pp, versus about 20pp between those architectures.

Why it matters: People shoot through glass all the time: shop windows, museum cases, car and plane windows. In the authors' tests, making the training reflections physically realistic mattered more than the choice of network. The system shows a preview in about 5 seconds on a laptop or phone and keeps full resolution and RAW color.

1,241,091 simulated training photos (256×256 pixels); no real reflection photos used for training (source: Sec. 5.1)
≈40 pct. points boost to earlier methods (Zhang, DSRNet, Zhu) from retraining on the RAW simulation, measured as improvement over the untouched photo on the simulated test set; the gaps among those designs are ≈20pp (source: Sec. 5.2, Table 2)
2.5M learned numbers (parameters) in the base model, versus 125M for DSRNet (source: Sec. 5.2, footnote 3)
4.5-6.5s time for a 1K preview on a MacBook or iPhone 14 Pro (source: Abstract)

A photo through glass is two pictures added together

In one sentence: A window lays a faint picture of what is behind you over what you are photographing; this paper learns to separate the two by practising on over a million fake mixtures (picked from millions of candidates) made the way glass really mixes light.

🧒 Explain it like I'm 8

Imagine two slide projectors shining on one screen, one showing a shop, the other a street. Where both shine, the light adds up. A window does the same to your photo. Removing a reflection means guessing which light came from which projector.

Toy example

The whole problem in one line

A made-up shop window.

t: the shop
behind the glass

+

r: the street
behind you

=

m: what the
camera records

What to notice: Given only m, is the bluish patch in the doorway part of the shop or the street? Several different splits add up to the same photo, so the computer has to learn what reflections usually look like.

Every dot of the photo (a pixel) is simply the light from the scene behind the glass plus the light of the reflection: \( m = t + r \), the transmission \(t\) plus the reflection \(r\).

Learning needs answer keys, such as a second shot with black material behind the glass. That fails if anything moves, so the largest real dataset has 14,952 pairs Sec. 2, yet some methods also pre-train on general photo collections of over a million images (e.g. ImageNet).

So earlier methods also train on fakes, blending two finished photos that have been white-balanced and tone-mapped: their numbers no longer measure light.

The key idea: add the fakes in RAW, where numbers are proportional to light, as glass does. Trained only on such fakes, the models still worked on real RAW photos the authors captured, including from cameras not used to build the training data Sec. 5.2.

Two more pieces come later: an optional photo looking the other way (e.g. the selfie camera) as a hint, and an upsampler that brings the result from the usual 256 pixels back to full size, returning both \(t\) and \(r\).

🔬 Go deeper: what earlier work did, and the six requirements

Prior synthesis. Most methods train on heuristically mixed pairs of tone-mapped images. Non-linear mixing models have been tried, and physically based methods exist (Kim et al.), but they still use tone-mapped images. Successful methods also need real ground-truth pairs, typically at about a 10:1 ratio of synthetic to real, and some pre-train on datasets larger than \(10^6\) (e.g. ImageNet). Lei and Chen subtract pairs of RAW images to suppress the reflection before converting to 8-bit; this paper works on RAW end-to-end.

Resolution. Most methods run at about \(256^2\) pixels and cannot be trivially scaled up; the paper argues previews need about 1K and final outputs beyond 4K.

Design targets (Sec. 1): handle typical consumer reflections; minimise user interaction; normal capture time (no video, bursts or stereo); results on screen in about 5 s; output at input resolution; and outputs that support editing (both \(t\) and \(r\)).

Why the fake reflections have to be mixed in RAW

In one sentence: Add the light before the camera "finishes" the photo, and fake reflections behave like real ones: true colors, strong in shadows, nearly invisible over bright lights.

How Adobe Camera RAW (ACR) finishes a photo:

Read the sensor

  1. 1 Linearize
  2. 2 Demosaic
  3. 3 Black level
  4. 4 Convert to XYZ mix here

Make it look good

  1. 5 White balance
  2. 6 Convert to RGB
  3. 7 Tone map, local contrast
  4. 8 Gamma

Steps 1–4 read the sensor and turn its numbers into standard colors that still measure light. Steps 5–8 make the photo look good, and from step 7 on, numbers stop adding like light.

Step 4 is the sweet spot: XYZ color is the same for every camera and comes before white balance, so a yellow-lit room and blue daylight keep their true colors.

What to notice: left, the street floods the dark doorway (A), spares the lamp (B), and grows with street brightness. Right, it spreads evenly and dims the lamp.

Fresnel physics says glass reflects only a small share of the light that hits it head-on (the paper gives up to −4 stops darker for angles of 0–45° from straight-on), and more at grazing angles, reaching about −1 stop at 83° Supp. B.1.

About 100 million mixtures were generated; about 10 million with a visible but readable reflection were kept Sec. 5.1; a tenth of those were rendered for training, giving 1,241,091 training photos at 256×256.

Does it matter? Training on photos gamma-compressed before mixing, or with all the physics removed, drops SSIM on t from 95.7% to about 89% Table 1 (see the evidence).

🔬 Go deeper: the pipeline, exposure and white balance

The ACR steps (paper's wording): 1. Linearize (e.g. remove vignetting and black levels); 2. Demosaic; 3. Subtract the scalar black level; 4. Convert to XYZ color; 5. White balance; 6. Convert to RGB color; 7. Dehaze, tone map (spatial adaptive highlights, shadows, clarity), enhance texture, adjust local contrast, hue, color tone, whites and blacks; 8. Gamma compress. Step 7 is proprietary, non-linear and spatially varying, so it cannot be modelled by a gamma curve. Steps 5–6 are linear but have removed the illuminant color; Step 3 keeps it but is in a sensor-specific basis. Step 4 is linear, sensor-independent and keeps the illuminant. This needs the ACR ColorMatrix path (to XYZ before white balance), which all DNGs must provide.

Exposure. With shutter \(s\), aperture \(n\), gain \(g\): \(e = s\,g/n^2\). Un-expose: \(t' = t/e_t\), \(r' = r/e_r\), \(m' = t' + r'\). Re-capture: \(m = C(m') = W e' m'\) with \(e' = \tau/\mathbb{E}[m']\), where \(\tau\) is sRGB 0.4 in linear units and \(W\) a 3×3 white balance in XYZ. If \(t\) or \(r\) has saturated pixels, \(e' = 1/\min(\max t', \max r')\).

White balance. The C5 auto white balancer (Afifi et al.) runs on the mixture in the camera space of \(t\), since \(t\) usually dominates. Mixtures whose new white point is extremely different from the as-shot one are culled. The same transform is applied to \(m, t, r\) and the context \(c\), then all go to linear sRGB.

About the lab. Toy values are invented. "Finished" means: auto exposure, gray-world white balance, a fixed shadow-lifting tone curve, gamma, 8-bit. The 8-bit blend uses weight \(w = \alpha^{1/2.2}\), \((1-w)\,t_8 + w\,r_8\); it is our simplified stand-in, not any one prior method's exact recipe. The verdicts at A and B come from how much adding the reflection changes each spot's on-screen brightness.

🔬 Go deeper: glass physics and the search settings

Fresnel. With incidence angle \(\theta_i\), \(\theta_i' = \arcsin(\sin\theta_i/\kappa)\):

\[ \alpha = \tfrac12\left(\frac{\sin^2(\theta_i-\theta_i')}{\sin^2(\theta_i+\theta_i')} + \frac{\tan^2(\theta_i-\theta_i')}{\tan^2(\theta_i+\theta_i')}\right) \]

\(r\) is scaled by \(\alpha\) (varying across the image), \(t\) by \(1-\alpha\); \(\kappa \sim U(1.47, 1.53)\). The lab uses \(\kappa = 1.5\), which gives about −4.6 stops at 0° and −4.3 at 45°; the paper's text describes 0–45° as "up to −4 stops".

Pose. Azimuth up to 50°, FOV \(\sim U(50°, 80°)\); pairs culled if inclinations differ by more than 15°, or \(|\phi| > 45°\), or roll \(|\rho| > 10°\). Double reflection: \(j_d = \alpha j + \beta j_w\), \(\beta = (1-\alpha)\alpha(1-\alpha)\); thickness \(U(8,20)\) mm, distance \(U(500,2000)\) mm, 50% double panes. Defocus: circle of confusion \(\delta = \frac{|d_o-d_f|}{d_o}\frac{f^2}{N(d_f-f)}\), depths \(U(1,100)\) ft, iPhone-like \(N \approx 1.6\), \(f \approx 26\) mm (35 mm equiv.); most reflections still come out sharp.

Search. Keep mixtures whose mean is well exposed, whose mean SSIM between \(m\) and \(t\) lies in [0.4, 0.94], and whose SSIM standard deviation is at least 0.05. Pairs are outdoor×indoor, indoor×outdoor and indoor×indoor (outdoor×outdoor omitted). The search bakes in priors: small, often yellow reflections of indoor lights over outdoor scenes; whole, often blue, outdoor scenes over interiors. Sources: MIT5K, RAISE, Laval Indoor (12,803 RAWs and 2,233 HDR panoramas); split 80/15/5 before simulation. 10% of the kept mixtures were rendered at 256² and 2048²; the 256² set has 1,241,091 train, 46,121 test, 8,991 validation.

How the remover works: a small separator, a helper photo, and a careful enlarger

In one sentence: a small network splits a shrunken photo into two layers, an optional photo of the scene behind you adds hints, and an enlarger restores full size.

Redrawn from the paper · Figure 2

The pipeline, one stage at a time

Click a stage, or press Next.

→
→
→
Stage 1 of 5

What to notice: the separating happens at 256 pixels.

Separating. The base model (the separator) has 2.5M learned numbers (parameters), vs 125M for DSRNet, a recent, much larger remover (2023) footnote 3.

The helper photo. The context photo usually doesn't show the same view as the reflection: the reflection is seen from a viewpoint shifted by twice the distance to the glass, a turned-around camera may share little of that view, and the photographer may block part of it Sec. 3.3. So c only hints at the reflected scene's colors and content, by turning the network's pattern detectors (feature channels) up or down. The gain is modest: +70 vs +66 on the paper's improvement-over-control score (see the evidence); in raw SSIM that is 95.7 vs 95.2 Table 2.

Enlarging. V-DESIRR, an earlier fast reflection remover (2021), repaints each bigger image from the previous one, so errors grow. The upsampler (the enlarger) instead enlarges a blurry mask of which details belong to t or r, and copies sharp detail through it from the photo at the next, twice-as-large pyramid level (lowercase t, r are the 256-pixel layers; uppercase T, R the full-size ones).

Toy example

Try it: enlarge the mask, not the picture

A pixel row is one horizontal line of dots across a photo; the bumps are two thin reflected lights. Press Bigger or Smaller.

2048 px

What to notice: repainting blurs edges and lets the lights creep back; mask-copying stays crisp. Real photos are messier (see where it still breaks).

Key result: enlarging true 256p layers to 2048p, PSNR on T is 47.77 dB, vs 42.24 for the best V-DESIRR and 43.29 without masks. On the base model's own outputs, what users get, the lead is small: 30.62 vs 30.27 dB Table 3. When upsampling ground-truth layers, the visible gain is fewer artifacts (Figure 5).

🔬 Go deeper: architecture, context modulation and training

Base model (Fig. S4). Backbone EfficientNet-B1 (first stride changed to 1, so no initial downsampling), fused by a BiFPN (EfficientDet D0) into 64 channels at 256p, with a fourth low-to-high pass. The context c goes through the same weights. The lowest-resolution features of m and c (64×4×4 each) feed a paired-channel MLP (64 tiny MLPs, one per channel pair) that predicts 64×K×2 affines. These drive two StyleGAN-style conv-mod-deconv operations in each "modulated merge" of the final low-to-high pass. Modulation is per-channel because c does not share content with m. The finishing head is Zhang et al.'s: 99 → 64 channels, 3×3 convs dilated (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 1), final 1×1 conv to 6 channels (t, r). t and r are predicted independently, not constrained to t + r = m, to decouple failures.

Base training. Losses of Zhang et al. (perceptual on gamma-compressed sRGB with VGG19, adversarial with a ResNet discriminator, exclusion with 5-tap derivatives, l1 reflection). Adam, lr 1e-4 (discriminator 5e-5), batch 32, 16 GPUs, 20 epochs, from random weights. In training, the reflection uses one half of a source photo and c is the other, non-overlapping half, so the model can't learn to find matching patches, which a real context photo usually wouldn't contain. For the context ablations, see the ablation in the evidence section.

Upsampler (Fig. S5). At each pyramid level, low-res (m, t, r) and high-res M are projected to features \(\phi\) by expand-contract convs (no batch norm). Affines predicted by a paired-channel MLP are applied to \(\phi_t, \phi_r\) and passed through a sigmoid to give per-pixel, per-channel masks \(I_t, I_r\), refined by a joint mask predictor. Then

\[ \Phi_T = \mathrm{up}_{2}(I_t) \odot \phi_M, \qquad \Phi_R = \mathrm{up}_{2}(I_r) \odot \phi_M \]

followed by finishing convs (128:(1,2), 96:(1,2,4,8), 64:(1,1)) that render T, R. Products, not sums, act as matchers: when features match, their product can be large regardless of sign, whereas a sum is large if either input is. Key assumption: which layer a feature belongs to varies slowly in space. Loss per output: 0.2 l1 + 0.2 l2 + 0.4 gradient + 0.8 LPIPS + 10 cycle-consistency \(\mathbb{E}|D(x'_H)-x_L|\), over three levels 128² → 1024². Adam lr 4e-4, batch 64, 32 A100s, about 40 epochs; then tuned on base-model outputs (19K examples, lr 2e-4).

Speed. Base model at 256×341: 0.96 s / 1.04 s on a 2021 M1 MacBook Pro / iPhone 14 Pro (footnote 3). End-to-end upsampling to a 1024×1364 preview: 4.52 s / 6.53 s (footnote 6).

Better fake data beat better networks

In one sentence: Retrained on the RAW simulation, earlier removers improved more than their designs differ, and the full system scored best.

The baselines are four earlier published removers: Zhang et al. (2018), CoRRN (2020), DSRNet (2023) and Zhu et al. (2023). "Ours" is the authors' model and "Ours+ctx" the same model with the helper photo.

The score is SSIM: a 0–100 similarity score between the recovered clean photo and the true one; 100 means identical. The control is the untouched photo. The chart shows improvement over the control: 0 means no better than doing nothing, 100 means perfect.

All these scores come from test images made by the same simulator used for training, because public test sets lack RAW files; the real-photo evidence is visual plus three ground-truth scenes Sec. 5.2.

From the paper · Table 2

Same networks, trained and tested on the RAW simulation

Switch between the published 8-bit models (scored on an 8-bit copy of the test set, converted with Adobe Camera RAW) and the same designs retrained and tested on RAW.

What to notice: RAW retraining moves bars more than switching networks. Below zero is worse than doing nothing. The two test sets have different controls, so compare improvements.

Zhang, DSRNet and Zhu each gain about 40 points of improvement, while the gaps among those three are only about 20 Sec. 5.2; CoRRN stays near the bottom either way.

The reverse test: train Ours+ctx on a simulation with every realism feature removed and images blended after gamma compression (Table 1, "All + G"), and its improvement falls from +70 to +24. Removing only the linear (gamma-free) mixing is about as damaging on its own (+70 → +21), the right-hand panel of the mixing lab. That is far larger than the context photo's +4 points Table 1, Sec. 5.2.

🔬 Go deeper: the ablations, and the ground-truth scene

Ablations (Table 1). Each row removes one realism feature: mixing gamma-compressed images (Gamma), exposing t and r separately (Exposure), unconstrained camera tilt and field of view (Pose), angle-dependent glass dimming (Fresnel), separate white balance (WB), no defocus blur or double reflection (Blur). "All − G" removes the other features but keeps linear mixing; "All + G" also mixes gamma-compressed images. The paper reports every difference as significant.

Is the context photo really used? Training and testing with a random context photo (Ours+rnd, +66) scores below Ours+ctx (+70), and no better than removing the context branch (Ours, +66); the paper reads this as Ours+ctx using the content of c. Feeding the true reflection as context at test time (Ours+rac) does not help, which suggests c and r need not match.

Reading "% vs ctrl". The paper does not spell out the formula. The printed values agree with the share of the control's remaining gap to a perfect score that a method closes, e.g. (95.7 − 85.8) / (100 − 85.8) ≈ 70%; that is our arithmetic check, not the paper's statement.

Where it still breaks

In one sentence: It fails where the photo has lost the information or the training data rarely went; because both layers come back, a person can fix the rest.

Think of the two slide projectors again: if one is blinding, the camera must shorten the exposure to fit the bright layer, so the dim one gets too few photons and sinks into the sensor's noise floor, or the bright one saturates the pixels. Then the hidden layer is gone, and the computer has to invent what was there, like patching a hole in a picture Sec. 5.2. If only one color channel clips, the content can sometimes still be recovered Sec. 5.2.

Toy example

Try it: when is the hidden layer still there?

Drag the slider to brighten the reflected lamp; switch how the camera sets exposure.

What to notice: push the lamp far enough and the subject sinks into the noise floor or clips. What was never recorded can only be guessed.

Other trouble spots:

  • Look-alike textures. Where textures of t and r overlap (a stone wall reflected over a dress, Figure 1), errors can occur. Color differences help separate them; without such differences, the model must repair or invent content Sec. 5.2.
  • Rare scenes. Interiors flooded by very strong lights, or rooms reflected over night-time cityscapes, give less consistent results Supp. F.2.
  • A blown-out helper photo. When the context photo's sky is saturated, its colors are recovered from the camera's as-shot settings; the authors believe this is why context sometimes leaves reflected cars or hurts the clean layer Supp. F.2.
  • Fine texture. The upsampler (the enlarger) copies sharp detail from the full photo, so reflection texture too fine to see at 256 pixels can be copied too Fig. S14.
  • What the paper does not show. On 8-bit photos, removal may be incomplete Fig. S13. No real-photo benchmark scores exist; the numbers come from the authors' simulated test set plus three ground-truth scenes, and the simulation assumes flat glass filling the view.

Because the reflection comes back as its own layer, a photographer can recolor it, move it, or paint back parts removed by mistake Sec. 5.4.

Keep in mind: partly thanks to RAW's extra bit depth, the models can uncover nearly invisible reflections, such as a photographer holding a phone in a framed print's glass Fig. S9; the authors note that privacy should be protected Sec. 6.

🔬 Go deeper: what these failures look like in the paper

Reflections are removed best when glass fills the view, as in the simulation; small local reflections (shiny cars, distant windows) are usually left alone, which the paper calls desirable Supp. F.2.

Glossary

8-bit image
A finished photo (like a JPEG) with 256 levels per color, already tone-mapped and white-balanced.
Base model
The first network: it looks at a small 256×256 version of the photo and predicts the clean layer and the reflection layer.
Context photo (c)
An optional extra photo pointed toward the reflected scene, such as from the selfie camera, that does not need to line up with the reflection.
Control
The untouched captured photo scored against the true clean (transmission) and true reflection images, as if a method did nothing at all.
Fresnel attenuation
The physics rule that says how much light glass reflects, which depends on the angle the light hits it.
Ground truth
The known correct answer, here the true clean and reflection images, used to score a method.
Improvement over control
The paper's score for how much of the way from the untouched photo (0) to a perfect result (100) a method gets.
Linear (scene-referred)
Pixel numbers that are directly proportional to real-world light, so adding two images adds their light.
Mixture (m)
The captured photo, equal to the transmission plus the reflection.
Noise floor
The faint random speckle every camera sensor records; detail darker than this level cannot be told apart from noise.
Ours / Ours+ctx
The authors' own model, without and with the optional context photo.
Parameters
The adjustable numbers a neural network learns during training; more parameters usually means a bigger model.
PSNR
A score in decibels for how close an image is to the correct one; higher is closer.
RAW photo
The camera sensor's nearly unprocessed data, where pixel values grow in proportion to the light that hit them.
Reflection (r)
The faint image of the scene on the photographer's side that the glass bounces into the camera.
Saturation
When a pixel receives more light than it can count, it records its maximum value and the true brightness is lost.
SSIM
A similarity score between two images, shown here as a percentage, where 100 means identical structure.
Stop
A photography unit of brightness: one stop darker means half as much light.
Tone mapping
The non-linear brightness and contrast adjustments a camera or editor applies to make a photo look good on a screen.
Transmission (t)
The scene behind the glass that the photographer actually wants.
Upsampler
The part of the system that turns the small 256-pixel results into full-resolution images.
White balance
A color correction that makes white objects look white by removing the tint of the light source.
XYZ color space
A standard, camera-independent way of describing color based on human vision, used here to mix images from different cameras.

How this page was made

This explainer was written by a team of AI agents. A lead editor read the paper and planned the page; experts wrote the sections: RAW color pipeline and glass optics expert (A photo through glass is two pictures added together, Why the fake reflections have to be mixed in RAW); Neural image-restoration architect (How the remover works: a small separator, a helper photo, and a careful enlarger); Evaluation and data-visualization specialist for image restoration (Better fake data beat better networks, Where it still breaks). The page was then revised over 1 round using feedback from simulated readers (Maya, 8, reading with her dad, Jordan, 15, a high-school student, Prof. Elena Rossi, 55, a professor in the field, Margaret, 70, a retired librarian), reviews by the experts of each other's sections, and a fact-checker that compared every section with the paper.

It can still contain mistakes: the original paper is the authoritative source. Anything marked Toy example is a simplified teaching illustration with made-up numbers, not a result from the paper. Figures marked From the paper are reproduced from it.
